caseNote: 가상 사례 (주방 리모델링 시공업체, 생활용품 매장) · 모든 기간과 상황은 설명용
insight: 계획의 가치는 미래를 맞히는 데 있지 않고, 긴 대기와 '이게 끝나야 시작할 수 있는' 순서를 아직 싸게 대응할 수 있을 때 찾아내는 데 있다.
misconception: 어차피 상황은 바뀌니 계획은 시간 낭비이고, 일단 빨리 시작하는 게 낫다.

sources.text: 프로젝트 관리의 표준 개념 (작업 분해, 선후 관계, 리드타임, 담당자 지정)
모든 사례와 기간은 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 주방 상판(석재)은 보통 하부장 설치 후 실측(템플릿)을 하고 그 뒤에 제작·설치하는 것이 일반적인 관행입니다. 제작 기간은 업체와 소재에 따라 며칠에서 몇 주까지 다양합니다. 카드의 '약 3주'는 가상 사례의 설정이며 일반 통계로 제시하지 않았습니다.
가상 일정 계산: 계획된 공사 4주 + 상판 제작·설치 대기 약 3주 = 약 7주. 훅과 3번 카드의 숫자가 일치하는지 확인했습니다.
소매 사례의 상자 인쇄 기간(6주), 개장까지 8주 등은 모두 가상 설정입니다. 앱 스토어 심사 등 소프트웨어 노트의 대기 항목은 기간을 명시하지 않고 일반적으로만 언급했습니다.

cards.title: The countertop nobody planned for
body: A family's kitchen remodel was supposed to take four weeks. The work itself did take four weeks. The kitchen took seven.
Nobody was slow. Nobody made a mistake on the job. Something simply had to wait for something else, and no one noticed until it was too late.

image.label: A half-finished kitchen with cabinets but no countertop
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 하부장은 설치됐지만 상판이 없는 주방. 싱크대가 바닥에 놓여 있고, 벽 달력에는 4주차 이후 3주가 빨간색으로 표시됨. 실제 브랜드 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Your crew is free on Monday.
body: You run a renovation business. A client wants a new kitchen in four weeks, and your crew can start Monday.
What do you do first?

options.text: Start demolition Monday. Momentum matters, and you'll sort out details as they come up
options.feedback: You gain an early start, but you discover each long wait only when you hit it, when the client is already living without a kitchen.

options.text: Start from the finished kitchen and work backward: what each step needs first, and what takes longest to arrive
options.feedback: It costs a few hours before any work begins. In return, slow items show up while you can still plan around them.

options.text: Build a detailed day-by-day schedule for your crew
options.feedback: Useful for the crew. But a schedule of your own work can still miss what suppliers need from you, and when.

cards.title: Week four brought the surprise.
body: The crew started Monday. Demolition, plumbing, wiring and cabinets all ran on time.
In week four, the stone fabricator came to measure the new cabinets for the countertop. Only then did anyone hear the next part: about three weeks to cut and install it.
The sink and dishwasher couldn't be connected until the countertop was in. So the family washed dishes in the bathtub for three more weeks.

image.label: Timeline showing a three-week gap after cabinets
image.brief: 가로 타임라인. 'Demolition', 'Plumbing & wiring', 'Cabinets'가 1~4주에 순서대로 놓이고, 그 뒤 'Measure countertop → 3-week wait → Install → Sink connected'가 이어짐. 3주 대기 구간을 강조색으로.

cards.title: Planning: start from done, work backward
body: **Planning** means turning a goal into the steps that get you there, in order, before you begin. You start from the finished result and ask, again and again, *what has to happen before this?*

Done on day zero, a plan would have shown the chain: sink needs countertop, countertop needs measured cabinets, then three weeks. The wait wouldn't vanish. But the contractor could have installed cabinets first, scheduled painting and lighting during the wait, and given the client the real date from the start.

cards.title: Four questions make a plan.
body: A useful plan answers four questions:
list: **What does done look like?** A kitchen the family can cook in, not just cabinets installed
**What must happen before each step?** The chain of *can't start until*
**What takes long to arrive?** Custom parts, permits, approvals, new hires
**Who owns each step?** A person's name, not *the team*
cards.callout: Most nasty surprises hide in the second and third questions.
cards.softwareNote: In software, the long waits often sit outside the team: an app store review, a customer's security check, a partner's data feed. Put those in the plan first.

cards.title: Same fact, different price.
body: A plan's main job isn't to predict the future. It's to **find problems while they're cheap**.
On day zero, the countertop wait cost almost nothing to handle: a different order of work and an honest date. In week four, the same fact cost three weeks and an unhappy client.
The information never changed. Only the moment it was found. That's why planning pays even when you know things will change.

cards.title: A plan can turn into a cage.
body: Plans start going out of date the day work begins. Treat yours as a working tool: look at it every week and change it when the facts change.
Don't plan every hour of month three either. Plan the next few weeks in detail and later stages roughly. Fine detail far ahead looks careful but mostly wastes time and gives false confidence.
How long each step takes is its own skill, covered in a later lesson.

cards.title: Now it's a shop.
body: You run a home goods store. In eight weeks you want a holiday gift corner: your own candles in custom boxes, new shelving and two seasonal staff.
Which approach helps most?

options.text: A shared to-do list of everything, ticked off as you go
options.feedback: It catches forgotten tasks. But a list has no order, so you may learn in week three that the boxes take six weeks to print.

options.text: Work back from opening day: box artwork before printing, shelving before setup, hiring before training. Start the slowest items this week, each with an owner
options.feedback: It takes an afternoon. It shows that printing and hiring are what could make you miss the season, while there's still time to act.

options.text: Order everything today and sort out the rest as it arrives
options.feedback: Ordering moves fast, but you may print boxes before the candle size is final, or buy shelving that doesn't fit the corner.

cards.title: Plan backward from done, before you start.
body: Planning isn't fortune-telling. It's finding the long waits and the *can't start until* moments while they're still cheap to handle.
**Try it today:** pick one project due in the next two months. Write the finished result at the top, then work backward. Circle anything that takes more than a week to arrive.
